title: Typewriter and Atlas
premise: In the river city of Vessengard, on the eve of the printers' revolution, Oscar Dravenmoor has spent twenty years as her father's silent apprentice, cutting typefaces by day and memorizing which questions never to ask. When an infant is abandoned at the print shop door wrapped in seditious broadsheets — the very evidence the Crown's censors have been burning — Oscar discovers the child is her father's granddaughter, left by a hanged pamphleteer with instructions to forget the face. To save the girl and her father's legacy, Oscar must smuggle the original plates and the child past three military checkpoints before the river ice breaks and the city seals itself. She succeeds at devastating cost: her father dies covering her escape, the revolution erupts without him, and Oscar, once defined by silence, chooses to sign her own name to the first free edition — a new typeface cut in her own hand, inherited and reinvented.
about_author: M. M. Galloway is the pen name of a former letterpress compositor who spent a decade restoring nineteenth-century printing equipment in Baltic port towns. Their fiction explores what working hands remember that official histories forget.

chapters.title: The Weight of Quiet Letters
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. We meet the Dravenmoor print shop two weeks before the ice breaks: her father cutting type, Oscar sorting type by feel in the dark, the city's censors growing bolder. Establish her rule of useful silences. Emotional beat: the ache of a talent — her own cutting hand — she has never been allowed to claim.

chapters.title: Left at the Door
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. A knock at midnight; an infant in a crate lined with banned broadsheets, a note reading 'forget the face.' Her father recognizes something and goes white, ordering her to burn everything. She secretly keeps one plate. Emotional beat: the first crack in twenty years of obedience.

chapters.title: What the Father Burned
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, with a flashback to her mother's disappearance. Oscar confronts her father; he admits the pamphleteer was his apprentice — and the child's mother was his daughter from a first life he buried. The plates are proof of a censorship conspiracy naming officials. Emotional beat: inheritance revealed as a burden, not a gift.

chapters.title: The First Checkpoint: Bridge of Weights
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. She hides the plates inside a delivery of hymnals and carries the child toward the river district, passing a checkpoint where a sympathetic guard — a former typesetter — lets her through but warns her she was recognized. Emotional beat: terror braided with the intoxicating discovery that strangers can be allies.

chapters.title: Ink Under the Fingernails
chapters.summary: Alternating POV with Ilse Varn, a censor's clerk hunting the missing plates. Ilse traces the broadsheets to Dravenmoor's foundry marks. Meanwhile Oscar shelters in a bookbinder's cellar and, for the first time, cuts a letter of her own design. Emotional beat: hunter and hunted both defined by their crafts.

chapters.title: The Second Checkpoint: The Salt Gate
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. The salt gate demands papers; Oscar forges them using her father's techniques, but the guard is Ilse's brother and nearly catches her. The baby's cry nearly betrays them; a smuggler named Rook covers for her at a price. Emotional beat: silence as a tool fails her for the first time — she must speak, and lie well.

chapters.title: Rook's Price
chapters.summary: Oscar and Rook's POV. Rook demands the plates' value in trade; Oscar negotiates by offering to teach him to read the very type he smuggles. Ilse closes in on the print shop. Emotional beat: unexpected tenderness, and guilt over trading her father's secrets to survive.

chapters.title: The Ice Begins to Sing
chapters.summary: Ilse's POV, then Oscar's. Ilse raids the shop; Oscar's father refuses to give up the location of the original plates, buying Oscar time with his arrest. The river ice cracks audibly across the city — the deadline made literal. Emotional beat: dread sharpening into resolve; the revolution's first fires on the far bank.

chapters.title: The Third Checkpoint: River of Names
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV. Climax. At the final checkpoint, Ilse herself stands guard. Oscar does not hide: she shows Ilse the plate — Ilse's own brother's name among the censored dead — and the child. Ilse steps aside as the ice breaks and the crossing becomes chaos. Emotional beat: the truth as the only passport that cannot be forged.

chapters.title: A Face Worth Remembering
chapters.summary: Oscar's POV, weeks later. Her father dies in custody before liberation; the city prints freely for the first time. Oscar sets the first edition herself, signs it, and cuts a new typeface named for the child, whose face she refuses to forget. Emotional beat: belonging claimed, identity inherited and remade, silence finally broken on her own terms.
